title: The Barmen Declaration (Condensed)
subtitle: The Confessing Church's 1934 stand against the Nazi capture of German Protestantism — six theses on why the church can have no Lord but Christ. The modern era's clearest word against every political captivity.
intro: In 1933 a movement calling itself the German Christians set out to merge Protestant faith with National Socialism — a swastika-friendly church with a heroic Aryan Jesus, racial exclusion written into church law, and the new regime hailed as God's fresh revelation in German history. Much of the institutional church went along. In May 1934, representatives of Lutheran, Reformed, and United churches met at Barmen and adopted a declaration — drafted principally by the theologian Karl Barth — refusing the merger at its root. It is not a full confession of faith; it is an emergency stand on one question: who rules the church? Its authors were not radicals, and many, including Dietrich Bonhoeffer's Confessing Church colleagues, paid in pulpits, prisons, and lives. The declaration was written in German; renderings vary, and the summary below is a close paraphrase of its six theses, each of which begins with Scripture and ends by rejecting a specific false doctrine. It is not the full text.
text:
The following is a condensed summary of the six theses. It is a faithful paraphrase, not the full text.

1. Jesus Christ, as witnessed to in Holy Scripture, is the one Word of God whom the church must hear, trust, and obey — in life and in death. Rejected: the false doctrine that the church could or should acknowledge, as a source of its proclamation beside this one Word, other events and powers, figures and truths, as God's revelation. The thesis is aimed at a church that had begun treating the nation's political moment as a second Bible.

2. As Jesus Christ is God's assurance of the forgiveness of all our sins, so and with equal seriousness he is God's mighty claim upon the whole of our life; through him comes joyful deliverance from this world's godless bonds into free, grateful service to his creatures. Rejected: the false doctrine that there are areas of life in which we belong not to Jesus Christ but to other lords — areas in which we do not need justification and sanctification through him. No sphere — political, racial, economic — is exempt from his lordship.

3. The church is the congregation of brothers and sisters in which Jesus Christ acts presently as Lord in Word and sacrament. With its faith as with its obedience, its message as its order, it must testify that it belongs to him alone. Rejected: the false doctrine that the church may abandon the form of its message and order to whatever it pleases, or to the changes in prevailing ideological and political convictions. The church's shape comes from its gospel, not from the age's fashions — a sentence with more addresses than 1934.

4. The church's offices are for the exercise of ministry entrusted to the whole congregation, not for domination. Rejected: the false doctrine that the church could give itself, or accept, special leaders vested with ruling powers — a direct refusal of the Führer principle imported into church governance.

5. The state, by divine appointment, has the task of providing for justice and peace in the still-unredeemed world, by the threat and use of force, and the church acknowledges this with gratitude and reverence. But: rejected is the false doctrine that the state should become the single and total order of human life, fulfilling the church's vocation as well — and equally rejected, that the church should take on the state's character, tasks, and dignity, becoming an organ of the state.

6. The church's commission is to deliver the message of the free grace of God to all people, in Christ's stead. Rejected: the false doctrine that the church, in human self-esteem, could place the Word and work of the Lord in the service of any arbitrarily chosen desires, purposes, and plans. The church is not for hire — not by a party, a program, or a people.

annotations.phrase: other events and powers, figures and truths
annotations.note: Barmen's first rejection is the whole document in miniature: the moment a nation, a leader, a race, or a political movement is received as revelation alongside Christ, the church has changed gods — whatever it still sings on Sunday. The German Christians did not think they were abandoning Jesus. They thought they were updating him.

annotations.phrase: areas of life in which we belong not to Jesus Christ but to other lords
annotations.note: The second thesis cuts both directions in every era: against the believer who exempts his politics from Christ's claim, and against the church that exempts its methods. A congregation may recite the creeds and still live thesis two's rejected doctrine every November.

The fifth thesis honors government as God's real but limited servant — and then draws the line the platform's whole diagnosis rests on: a church conscripted by state or party, of any flag or either party, has traded its commission for employment. Barmen indicts capture as such, not one direction of it.

annotations.phrase: paid in pulpits, prisons, and lives
annotations.note: Barmen is on this shelf because confession is not commentary: within a decade, signers and heirs of this declaration were banned from preaching, drafted, imprisoned, or executed — Bonhoeffer among the dead, hanged in April 1945. The document proves that the question this platform keeps asking — can a church refuse the nation's embrace and keep the faith? — has been answered in living memory, at cost.
